newsitem.title: GERMANY: French, Italians favour euro, Germans split - polls.
newsitem.headline: French, Italians favour euro, Germans split - polls.

text.p: Polls show that referendums on European monetary union would yield "yes" votes in France and Italy, a "no" in Britain and a race too close to call in Germany, busines daily Handelsblatt said on Thursday.

Polls conducted last month also showed majorities in all four nations -- including 79 percent of the Germans who were asked -- favoured national plebiscites on currency union, said Handelsblatt, which will publish the poll results on Friday.

Earlier on Thursday German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he opposed a referendum on introduction of a single European currency, the euro. Germany's constitution rules out such votes to avoid a repeat of the Weimar era's instability, he noted.

But Kohl said he was confident a clear majority of Germans would favour the euro in the end. "I am confident that when... people have all the information we will get a clear majority of the population for the euro," he told a news conference.

Only 43 percent of the Germans polled said they would vote for currency union, while 44 percent were against it, with 11 percent undecided, Handelsblatt said. The newspaper did not account for the remaining two percent of the German sample.

In Italy 71 percent and in France 61 percent said they would vote in favour of currency union. In Britain, 26 percent would support the euro in a referendum, while 56 percent said they would vote against.
Handlesblatt joined with Britain's Daily Telegraph and France's Le Figaro newspapers and Italy's L'Espresso news magazine to poll about 950 people in each country.
